blocks: Businesses combine natural resources, labour, capital, entrepreneurship and knowledge to create value. Retailers offer availability and convenience. Economic systems organise resources differently; inflation, employment and growth influence business decisions. Supply, demand and competition affect prices [1].

Concept Check, section 1.1: how do revenue, costs and profit differ? When a shopper buys bread at Magnum, the money received is revenue. The shop pays for the bread, wages and rent. Profit is what remains after all costs. Higher sales alone do not establish higher profit.

Company A is Carrefour SA, an international retailer with franchised operations: 15,415 stores under its banners at 30 June 2026 [2]. Company B is Magnum Cash&Carry, serving households and businesses in Kazakhstan. Magnum reported over 200 stores on 1 July 2026 [3]. Carrefour provides documented practices to compare; Magnum provides the local setting. The question is whether assisted ordering or search could improve service at an acceptable cost.

The inflation evidence makes affordability relevant, but store sales and shopper feedback are needed to identify which products people will buy.

weeks.topic: Business environment and sustainability: economic systems, ethics, global markets and SDGs
weeks.title: Ethics and stakeholders
blocks: Ethics concerns right and wrong. Utilitarianism weighs overall consequences, while duties and rights protect people whose interests might otherwise be overlooked. Managers influence behaviour through their example, training and reporting arrangements [1].

CSR includes economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities. These operate together [13]. Concept Check, section 2.3: give an example of legal but irresponsible behaviour [1]. A lawful promotion could encourage customers to buy food they cannot use. Donations would not remove that problem.

Comparative advantage means specialising where opportunity cost is lower. Imports come from abroad; exports go abroad. Trade balance is exports minus imports. Currency depreciation, transport costs and trade barriers can make foreign purchases more expensive [1].
Company B is Magnum Cash&Carry; Company A is Carrefour. Magnum’s history records entry into Uzbekistan in 2021 [14]. This establishes regional experience, not export volumes.

The proposed use is catalogue search. Magnum Club’s policy lists purchase histories and location data [15], creating a tension between useful recommendations and privacy. My priorities are customers, who bear direct harm; regulators, who influence permitted processing; and employees, who correct mistakes. Suppliers need fair visibility. Owners need a viable trial, while communities bear waste consequences.

Checks on 20 September 2026 matched the Uzbekistan entry year to Magnum’s history [14], data categories to policy section 4.3 [15], and Hopla’s launch to Carrefour’s release of 8 June 2023 [12]. The release gives no measured error rate or staff savings. I therefore removed implied proof of effective oversight. NIST supports named responsibilities and training [16]; it does not certify Magnum.
The evidence refines my initial view: faster service matters only if shoppers can rely on it. The checks distinguish company announcements from measured performance.

PILOT catalogue search after privacy review. The digital team should test Kazakh and Russian questions against available products, comparing errors and staff correction time with ordinary search. A service manager should resolve complaints and pause the trial after harmful recommendations. DELAY purchase-history personalisation until its purpose and benefit are demonstrated.

Carrefour also proposes recipes using leftover ingredients [12]. Magnum could adapt this idea to products approaching expiry, with stock and safety checks. Store managers should compare discarded food per unit sold before and during the trial, linking it to SDG 12.3 [17]. This is a proposed measure, not a reported result.
Carroll [13], NIST [16] and UN Goal 12 [17] extend the Evidence Folder. Company sources are reused. Course material: Chapter 2 and 3 slides and BA Week 2 Practice 2, slides 7–16.

weeks.topic: Ownership, entrepreneurial mindset and business models
weeks.title: Ownership and business model
blocks: Ownership affects control, finance and risk. A sole proprietor has direct control but unlimited personal liability. Partners share resources and decisions; liability depends on the form. A corporation is a separate legal entity, with ownership held through shares. Entrepreneurs seek opportunities under uncertainty, while intrapreneurs develop ideas within an existing organisation [1].

Concept Check, section 5.1: what differentiates an entrepreneur from a small-business owner? Entrepreneurship emphasises innovation and growth; an owner may instead prioritise a stable operation. At Magnum, an employee proposing a forecasting trial would be acting as an intrapreneur.

Carrefour SA operates an international retail model that includes franchises [2]. Magnum identifies itself as an LLP [15]. Kazakhstan’s partnership law generally limits participants’ risk to their contributions, subject to exceptions, and makes their general meeting the highest governing body [18]. This legal form does not reveal Magnum’s beneficial owners or its internal approval limits.

Magnum creates value by making goods available to households and business customers [14]. Sales generate revenue; purchases, wages, premises and logistics consume it. Forecasting could reduce tied-up stock and waste, while catalogue search could make shopping easier. Both also add software and staff costs. Magnum Club already provides digital loyalty interaction [15], although the policy does not establish AI deployment.

weeks.topic: Management and leadership: planning, organising, leading and motivating
weeks.title: Management, responsibility and human–AI task allocation
blocks: Management connects planning, organising, leading and controlling. Setting a target is only the first step: managers must provide resources, explain responsibilities and respond when results fall short. Chapter 7 distinguishes authority from responsibility and explains how reporting relationships support coordination [1].

Concept Check, section 7.4: how does the chain of command clarify reporting relationships? For the proposed Magnum trial, staff would report stock discrepancies to the category manager. The manager could obtain IT support without passing the purchasing decision to the software. Participative leadership would let store employees challenge forecasts using what they see on the shelves [1].

Magnum’s retail and wholesale activities make replenishment a relevant process [14]. I propose a six-month forecasting trial in one store and product category, with the category manager accountable for ordering. Week 3 identified inaccurate promotion and stock records as a reason to delay the trial. Those records must therefore be checked first.
The matrix separates producing a recommendation from committing money. It describes proposed roles; public company material does not establish Magnum’s current allocation of these tasks.
Approve the final order and handle exceptional commitments.
The category manager checks stock, shelf life and budget, records the decision and remains accountable [1], [16], [22].
Interpret promotion effects and unusual demand.
AI highlights patterns; staff add local knowledge and challenge misleading suggestions. Store feedback informs the manager’s decision [1].
Produce demand forecasts and draft order quantities.
Carrefour’s forecasting example supports testing this use [20]. The manager checks inputs, unusual quantities and supplier limits before accepting or changing each order.
Check missing fields and timestamps; record versions and approvals.
These are fixed rules, not AI purchasing decisions. Failed checks block the draft and notify staff. Logs make errors traceable [16].

If records disagree or a forecast fails, staff stop the affected recommendation and alert the category manager. Unresolved supply problems go to the supply-chain lead; technical faults go to IT. Staff use a physical stock count and verified sales to prepare a manual order for the same manager’s approval. Training should include rejecting a poor forecast and practising this fallback.

The course text was checked for management functions, participative leadership and reporting relationships [1]. NIST supports explicit responsibilities and staff training [16]. The SAS announcement describes Carrefour’s forecasting work, but it does not establish Magnum’s performance or guarantee savings [20].
The important distinction is authority: automating calculations does not mean delegating the right to place an order.

PILOT Carrefour’s forecasting approach after reconciling local data [20]. Adapt it to Magnum’s category, promotions and supplier lead times. Keep final approval with a named manager. Do not expand if staff cannot explain the forecasts, correct errors or operate the manual process.

The Evidence Folder links the textbook [1], Magnum’s company description [14], NIST [16] and the SAS announcement [20] to their specific claims. The proposed management roles are an application of these sources, not a published Magnum organisation chart.
This record supplies the human–AI operating model for Assignment 2 and the capstone.

weeks.title: Replenishment, controls and performance
blocks: Operations management coordinates people, materials and information to deliver a useful service at an acceptable cost. Resource planning balances availability against the cost of holding stock. A process map shows where work passes between people and where a delay or error can affect the whole service [1].

Concept Check, section 10.4: how is technology used in resource planning? It can combine sales and stock data to support purchasing. The benefit depends on accurate inputs and workable decisions. Faster calculations alone will not fill an empty shelf, and a forecast should not become a purchase without review.

The process is replenishment of one product category in one Magnum store. Its retail activities and product acceptance rules establish the context [14], [22]. The current-state sequence below is an evidence-informed baseline to confirm with staff; it is not an observed account of Magnum’s internal procedures. The proposed bottleneck is reconciling stock and promotion information before deciding quantities.
Automated: validate sales and stock inputs; block failed checks.
Estimate demand and order quantity using the existing method.
AI Executes with Human Review: forecast demand and draft quantities.
An authorised manager approves the order.
Human + AI: staff interpret promotions and supplier constraints. Human Only: the category manager checks exceptions and approves or changes the order.
Send the order and receive goods.
Send only the approved order and receive goods.
Check shelf availability and costs. Automated logs preserve inputs, revisions and approvals for review.

If records disagree or a forecast fails, staff stop the affected recommendation and alert the category manager. Unresolved supply problems go to the supply-chain lead; technical faults go to IT. Staff prepare a manual order from verified sales and a physical stock count. The category manager approves it and authorises any restart after correction. No unapproved order is sent [16].

The following six-month pilot targets are proposals, not Magnum results. Establish a baseline before starting, use the same products and checking schedule, and compare results with the existing ordering method.
Available product checks ÷ all scheduled checks × 100. Target: at least 98%.
Sum of absolute forecast errors ÷ sum of actual units sold × 100. Target: a 10% relative reduction from baseline.
Proposed reductions of 10% each in expired/damaged stock value and staff cost per order. Include software, training and correction costs when assessing net benefit.

Lost sales during stockouts can conceal demand, so WAPE must be interpreted alongside shelf availability. The category manager should review exceptions daily and trends weekly, using store feedback to explain unusual results [1].

Carrefour’s documented forecasting initiative makes PILOT a defensible transfer decision [20]. Week 3’s stock-data problem remains a stop condition. Expand only if availability reaches the target, forecast error improves, net benefit remains positive and staff can use the fallback. weeks.topic: Markets and customers: marketing functions, selling strategies and the buying process
weeks.title: Customer value, pricing and promotion
blocks: Marketing starts from customer value: the benefits a customer receives compared with the price and effort of buying. A firm combines product, price, place and promotion to deliver that value to a chosen target market [1]. Pricing decides how much of that value the firm captures, and promotion informs, persuades and reminds; sales promotion adds a short-term reason to buy now [1].

Concept Check, section 11.9: what is the difference between penetration pricing and price skimming? Penetration sets a low price to win market share quickly; skimming starts high and lowers the price later. A mature grocery category leaves little room to skim, so value depends on clear, credible offers.

Concept Check, section 12.8: how does sales promotion differ from advertising? Advertising builds awareness over time through paid media; sales promotion offers a temporary incentive, such as a discount, coupon or bonus, to trigger an immediate purchase. Magnum’s weekly Пайда programme is a sales promotion.

Magnum’s target segment is budget-conscious households doing a weekly family shop. Annual inflation was 9.8% in August 2026 [4], and Magnum Club reports more than 2 million members [24]. Пайда listed 51 products for 15–21 October, discounted by 18–53% [23]. Of the six products reduced by 50% or more, four were household or personal-care items; staples in the list (eggs, bananas, chicken fillet) were reduced by only 18–22% [23].

The friction point lies between consideration and purchase. The Пайда page attracts attention, but its “up to 60%” promise was not met that week, and it offers no store link or Magnum Go button [23], [25]. The Week 6 artifact therefore compared two ways of writing the same weekly message from the same 51-product list.
Prices and dates match the catalogue
Met: checked against the saved list
Met: nearest store or Magnum Go
Met: facts from the list only

Limitations: the test covered one week and one message, the baseline’s authorship was assumed, and no customer response was measured. blocks: Data are raw facts; information is data organised so that someone can act on it. A management information system turns transaction data into reports and decision support; its value depends on accurate inputs, clear responsibilities and protection against unauthorised access, malware and human error [1].

Concept Check, section 13.1: how do data and information differ? A list of 51 products with prices is data; a verified message telling a family which deal saves the most, until when and where to buy is information. Data become valuable when they support a better decision.

Concept Check, section 13.5: why are privacy advocates alarmed by data warehouses and data mining? Combining records from many sources can reveal detailed profiles that customers never agreed to share, and a larger store of data makes a breach more harmful.

The decision continues Week 6: each week, which Пайда deal to feature and which message to send to which Magnum Club segment, using the pricing system, the Magnum Club CRM and app, Magnum Go, an approved AI tool and a dashboard. Internal system names are not public, so roles are assumed [23]–[25].

In the proposed workflow the AI tool receives only the public promo list and drafts three messages; segments are built inside the CRM using consent flags. A copywriter checks every price, date and claim, a native speaker checks the Kazakh text, and the brand manager approves. Personal data stay in Kazakhstan, where Law 94-V requires them to be stored [7].

Uncertain cases go to the brand manager, personal-data issues to the person responsible for personal data, and AI-labelling questions to legal. If the AI tool or the check fails, the copywriter uses an approved template with the same checks; if the CRM is down, no push is sent. This fallback is not hypothetical: on 17 October Carrefour’s Hopla assistant showed a loading error twice [29].

The legal points were read on adilet.zan.kz: Law 94-V, articles 7, 12 and 16 [7], and AI Law No. 230-VIII, articles 17, 18 and 21 [27]. The CNIL decision was read in EDPO’s unofficial English translation, which links to the CNIL original [26]. The risk ratings are qualitative judgements. Open question: whether AI-drafted copy edited by people needs an AI label under article 21; legal should decide before a pilot.

ADOPT the controls, DELAY the personalisation. Carrefour’s Hopla uses purchase history but warns users not to enter personal data [29], and the CNIL fined Carrefour France €2.25 million partly for keeping the loyalty data of 28 million inactive customers for 5–10 years [26]. Magnum should first set retention limits, an AI-use notice and fast opt-out, adjusted to Kazakhstan’s storage rule and AI Law [7], [27], before any personalisation with purchase history.

weeks.title: Financial ratios and their verification
blocks: Accounting turns transactions into three statements. The balance sheet shows what a firm owns and owes on one date; the income statement shows revenue, expenses and profit over a period; the statement of cash flows shows where cash came from and where it went [1]. Ratio analysis is the framework for reading them: it expresses figures as proportions so that firms of different sizes, or one firm in different years, can be compared. Liquidity ratios ask whether short-term bills can be paid, profitability ratios how much of each sale becomes profit, activity ratios how efficiently assets are used, and debt ratios how much of the firm is financed by borrowing [1].

Concept Check, section 14.7: how can ratio analysis be used to interpret financial statements? A ratio is meaningful only against a benchmark: the same firm in another year, a competitor or a target. It shows where to ask questions rather than giving the answer. Debt ratios worry lenders because a heavily borrowed firm has less room to repay if sales fall.

Concept Check, section 14.8: how are automation and cloud tools changing accounting? Routine posting and calculation are increasingly automated, so the accountant’s work moves towards checking the data and explaining what the numbers mean for a decision.

Magnum Cash&Carry is a private partnership and, unlike Carrefour, publishes no balance sheet or income statement that I could find. Its only public financial data are Forbes Kazakhstan’s rankings of the largest private companies, which give revenue and headcount but list net profit as “no data” [31], [32]. I therefore calculated the ratios these data allow, compared them with an AI-supported interpretation of Forbes’s Magnum profile [33], and audited every difference.

The audit separates two kinds of work. The arithmetic was right every time; every problem concerned the period, rounding, inflation or missing data, which required reading the source.

What did I check? The fiscal year behind Magnum’s revenue of 453.13 billion tenge. Against which source? The methodology of Forbes’s 2025 ranking, which ranks companies by 2024 revenue and was prepared with Adata.kz [31]. What did I find? The company profile labels the same figure “2025” [33], so a comparison with annual inflation would have been one year out. I also checked the 10,000 headcount against Magnum’s careers site, which uses the same round number for the whole company [36], and took 2024 inflation of 8.6% from the Bureau of National Statistics as reported by BES.media [35]. Magnum’s exit from Uzbekistan in 2025 [34] and Kaspi’s 2023 purchase of Magnum’s e-commerce business [31] may change what later figures cover; without statements I cannot measure that effect.

The logic transfers to Magnum’s head office: AI can do the calculation and the first draft. The implementation must change. blocks: Human resource management plans the people a firm needs, then recruits, selects, trains, appraises and pays them [1]. Job analysis studies what a job involves: the job description lists its tasks, and the job specification lists the skills a person needs to do them. Training and development builds those skills on or off the job, and performance appraisal checks whether the job is being done well. A knowledge worker is valued for applying what they know rather than for physical output [1]. This week’s framework is the course’s four capability groups: human, business, digital and meta-capabilities.

Concept Check, section 8.4: how is technology affecting off-the-job training? Online courses and simulations let people train without leaving work and repeat an exercise until they can do it. Kazakhstan’s AI-Sana programme shows the scale: about 650,000 students completed a basic course in working with neural networks in its first stage [42]. When almost every graduate has taken such a course, basic AI use stops being a distinction.

Concept Check, section 9.8: how do knowledge workers differ from traditional employees? Their value depends on judgment and learning, so firms keep them through development and responsibility rather than pay alone.

The Career Capability Portfolio maps the four capability groups against my Week 4 operating model, in which Magnum’s category manager keeps order approval and AI drafts forecasts under review. Magnum separates office and store vacancies, says it trains new staff itself and runs Magnum Start for students and graduates [36]. Exposure follows international evidence: clerical work is the most exposed to generative AI, although transformation is more likely than replacement [40], and seven in ten employers rate analytical thinking as essential [41].

weeks.topic: Capstone project: putting it all together
weeks.artifact: 12-month roadmap and transfer stress test, no new record

blocks: Magnum should concentrate on reliable product availability and affordable shopping, testing AI where it can help with these tasks. Magnum Cash&Carry is a Kazakhstan-based retailer that also serves business customers through wholesale operations [1]. Carrefour, Company A, provides a comparison because its public reporting covers an international retail business with franchised operations [2]. This report focuses on Magnum’s Kazakhstan business. Carrefour’s experience can suggest what to test, but cannot establish what Magnum will earn from it.

The economic issue carried forward from Weekly Record 1 is affordability. Kazakhstan’s annual inflation was 9.8% in August 2026, according to the Bureau of National Statistics release of 1 September [3]. This makes price and purchasing decisions important, although it does not tell us which products Magnum shoppers will choose. Store sales and customer feedback are needed before changing an assortment.

BNS also reported that e-commerce represented 14.3% of Kazakhstan’s retail trade in 2025 [4]. This includes marketplaces and is not a grocery-specific measure. It supports examining digital shopping, rather than assuming customers want an AI assistant. SMALL’s retail and technology presence provides a relevant local comparison [5]. Magnum therefore needs to judge any proposed improvement against ordinary shopping and ordering, including whether the extra cost is justified. A convenient search tool has limited value when the recommended item is unavailable.

Weekly Record 2 prioritises customers, regulators and employees for the proposed catalogue-search trial. Customers bear the direct consequences of unsuitable recommendations. Regulators influence permitted data processing, while employees must identify errors and handle complaints. Suppliers need accurate descriptions and fair visibility; owners need a viable business. Communities are affected by waste. Magnum’s corporate rules address customer safety, supplier selection and reporting concerns [6]. These commitments establish expectations, but do not show how consistently individual stores meet them.

The clearest ethical tension concerns loyalty data. Magnum Club offers bonuses and offers based on customer interests, and its privacy policy describes purchase and application information [7]. Additional personalisation might encourage sales while making shoppers less comfortable about how much the company knows. Kazakhstan’s Personal Data Law establishes principles including lawfulness and confidentiality [8]. Before any new use, the privacy and legal teams should review its purpose, access permissions and customer choices. A published policy alone cannot establish that a proposed AI workflow meets these obligations.

Global trade adds another responsibility. Magnum’s supplier portal provides routes for resident and non-resident suppliers [9]. Currency changes, transport costs and uncertain deliveries could affect purchases, although this does not establish an import share or an actual disruption. Procurement should compare delivered cost and reliability while preserving product standards and fair treatment. Cheap sourcing loses value if goods arrive too late or spoil before sale.

The CSR discussion in Weekly Record 2 distinguishes viable operations, legal compliance, fair treatment and voluntary community support. Charitable giving cannot compensate for misleading recommendations or ignored complaints. For the search trial, the digital team should compare errors in Kazakh and Russian, and a service manager should own corrections and escalation. Staff should be able to challenge suggestions without pressure to approve them. Any food-waste claim needs a baseline and a consistent measure. Appendix Table 2 applies these obligations to the proposed search process. Expansion should depend on reliable service and acceptable costs, with unresolved privacy or safety concerns stopping the trial.

Magnum creates value by bringing products together where households and businesses can buy them. Its retail and wholesale activities serve different purchasing needs [1]. A household buys a basket for personal use; a business may need repeated supplies. In both cases, availability and convenience matter. Revenue comes from sales. After paying for goods, the remaining margin must cover wages, premises, logistics and other operating costs before there is profit. An increase in sales is therefore not sufficient evidence that a new service pays for itself.

Stock connects this model to risk. Goods waiting on shelves tie up money, while missing products can lose a sale. Perishable goods add the possibility of waste. Assisted forecasting could help managers decide what to order, but poor stock records would also make its recommendations unreliable. The comparison should include forecast errors, unavailable products, waste and staff time. These are proposed measures, not reported results for Magnum.

The company identifies its legal form as an LLP, or ТОО [7]. Under Kazakhstan’s partnership law, participants generally risk their contributions, subject to statutory exceptions; the partnership remains responsible for its obligations. The participants’ general meeting is its highest governing body [10]. This separates ownership from daily execution without removing management accountability. The sources used here do not establish Magnum’s beneficial owners or internal approval limits, so neither is assumed.

Weekly Record 3 treats a category manager’s trial as intrapreneurship within Magnum. A budget and stopping condition allow an idea to be tested without changing ownership. Magnum Club demonstrates digital customer interaction [7], but does not establish AI deployment. Combining the three records supports a narrower investment decision: improve ordering before expanding personalisation. If stock records prove unreliable during promotions, the verdict changes from pilot to delay until records are reconciled. Appendix Table 3 tests this changed assumption against costs and service outcomes.

Adapt product search. Carrefour introduced Hopla in France in June 2023 [11]. Its later announcement describes Hopla+ and shopping through ChatGPT [12]. Magnum could adapt the underlying catalogue search rather than copy the whole service. Questions in Kazakh and Russian should return products from the relevant catalogue with accurate availability. Ordinary search and staff assistance should remain available. The benefit depends on successful shopping, not on how fluent the reply sounds.

Pilot demand forecasting. Carrefour and SAS described using AI to support its supply chain [13]. This supports testing the process, not assuming the same return at Magnum. A trial should compare assisted forecasts with current ordering under comparable conditions. Category managers should approve orders and record corrections, including problems caused by promotions or missing stock data.

Adopt the principle of supplier accountability. Carrefour’s supplier ethics charter covers working conditions, safety and confidential reporting [14]. Magnum already has corporate rules [6], so the useful transfer is to check that purchasing decisions and complaint handling put those commitments into practice. It is not a reason to introduce another policy without checking the existing arrangements.

Delay additional personalisation based on shopping histories. Carrefour’s newer shopping service includes purchase-history suggestions [12], but Magnum should first establish a clear purpose, acceptable data handling and a benefit beyond its existing loyalty offers. Reject fully autonomous order approval at this stage. This is a boundary for the proposed Magnum trial, not a claim that Carrefour operates without people. Local performance, costs and accountability remain unresolved. These different verdicts reflect the risks of each activity rather than a general decision to accept or refuse AI.

First, the inventory team and category managers should select a manageable product category and pilot assisted forecasting. Keep current ordering as the comparison and retain manual approval. Success would mean fewer stockouts and less waste, with benefits exceeding software and staff costs [13].

Second, the digital team should test catalogue search with equivalent Kazakh and Russian shopping questions. Store staff should check matches and availability, comparing errors across languages. The service manager should record corrections and complaints; expand only if shoppers find suitable products more reliably than with ordinary search [11], [12].

Third, the privacy and legal teams should review proposed uses of Magnum Club data before adding personalisation. Document the purpose, access and customer choices. Successful completion means that unnecessary data are excluded and the proposed use has an approved legal basis [7], [8].

Finally, procurement and store managers should review supplier complaints and delivery exceptions together. Record resolution and recurrence. Success would mean fewer repeated issues and quicker resolution while product standards are maintained. This tests whether Magnum’s existing commitments influence purchasing and service [6].

AI Executes with Human Review covers producing a demand forecast and draft quantities.

Automated covers fixed checks for missing fields and stale data, plus logging approved orders.
These routine rules require no model judgment.
The allocation follows the textbook’s planning and control cycle:
set standards, compare outcomes and correct deviations.

NIST supports defined oversight, training and a non-AI alternative.

My verdict is PILOT.

visuals.title: Company B: Magnum Cash&Carry and the value it promises
visuals.comment: Magnum sells savings and loyalty: a weekly discount catalogue, Magnum Club bonuses and offers such as a 30% Nivea bonus [28]. With 9.8% annual inflation [4], saving is the core household value. Club membership (2M+) is Magnum’s own figure [24], so the essay relies on customer-facing evidence.

visuals.title: The customer journey and where it breaks
visuals.comment: Value appears at every stage, but the weak link is between Consideration and Purchase. Shoppers can compare 51 deals [23] yet are not told where or how to buy, despite four store formats [28] and Magnum Go delivery [25]. This gap, not discount depth, is the essay’s problem.

visuals.title: The weekly Пайда page: strong attention, no next step
visuals.comment: The Пайда page confirms the gap. Its banner earns attention, but the promise of “up to 60%” was not met that week (maximum 53%), and the only instruction is to “keep following Пайда” [23]. For budget shoppers this weakens trust and leaves no next step.

visuals.title: What the 51 Пайда deals actually offer
visuals.comment: The data refine the insight: four of the six deepest discounts are non-food, while eggs, bananas and chicken fillet sit at 18–22% [23]. The biggest discount is not the most useful one for a family basket, so a tool ranking offers by discount alone would repeat this pattern.

visuals.title: Same task, two approaches: the method
visuals.comment: To test whether AI helps, both approaches used the same 51-product list and four criteria [23]. The baseline is Magnum’s published text, assumed human-written; the AI draft followed a prompt restricted to list facts. The method is transparent but small: one week, one message.

visuals.title: The result: same task, two outputs
visuals.comment: The AI draft met all four criteria, the baseline one. AI made the message specific and actionable, but customer response was not tested. The draft also named Magnum Go [25] without confirming Пайда prices apply there [23] and chose a non-food deal, echoing Visual 4. Human review remains essential.

visuals.title: Proposed workflow with a human gate
visuals.comment: The workflow places a human gate before anything reaches customers: AI drafts, a copywriter checks every price and claim, and the brand manager approves. Monitoring feeds the next brief; a manual template keeps campaigns running if the tool fails. This is a proposed pilot, not Magnum’s current system [7], [27].

visuals.title: From data to information, inside Kazakhstan’s rules
visuals.comment: The data boundary is a design choice, not paperwork. Only the public promo list reaches the AI tool; member data stays in Kazakhstan under the Personal Data Law’s consent and transfer rules [7]. The AI Law also requires telling users when services use AI [27].

visuals.title: Four risks, each with a control and an owner
visuals.comment: Privacy is the most serious risk: a leak of members’ data cannot be undone, and Kazakh law sets strict conditions [7], [24]. Its control keeps personal data out of prompts. An automatic price check plus sign-off controls reliability; a weekly food-staple rule controls bias. Residual risk: human error and unclear AI-labelling rules [27].

visuals.title: What Magnum should take from Carrefour, and on what terms
visuals.comment: Carrefour’s Hopla shows the opportunity and the cost [29]. Magnum should adapt AI content generation, used on 2,000+ Carrefour product sheets [12], adding fact checks and Kazakh review; adopt the data controls Carrefour introduced after a €2.25 million CNIL fine [26]; and delay purchase-history personalisation and ChatGPT shopping [19]. Next: a four-week pilot tracking orders and price complaints.

sections: I agree with the claim only in a qualified form. AI will make business graduates more valuable to Magnum Cash&Carry if they can verify, interpret and take responsibility for what AI produces; it will make them less valuable if they only produce routine numbers and reports, because that is the part AI already does well. My Week 8 ratio audit and Week 9 capability map point the same way: value moves from producing analysis to judging it. The cost, which the counterargument presses, is that this may mean fewer graduate jobs, each demanding more.

Magnum is a private partnership and publishes no balance sheet or income statement that I could find, so my Week 8 ratios rest on Forbes Kazakhstan’s rankings of the largest private companies [31], [32]. Revenue per employee in 2024 was 47.2 million tenge (453.13 billion tenge divided by 9,599 employees), verified against the 2025 ranking’s methodology, which states that it uses 2024 revenue [31]. An AI-supported interpretation of the same data got every calculation right, and my independent calculation matched it to two decimals (Appendix A). Its problems were judgments. It compared ranking years instead of fiscal years. It read the rise in revenue per employee as “a sign of higher productivity”, although its largest jump, 40% in one year, falls in 2023, whose headcount is a round 10,000, the figure Magnum’s careers site uses [36]. It said revenue had “slipped only about 2%”, whereas the verified years show a 5.6% nominal fall, about 13% in real terms after 8.6% inflation [35]. It inferred “thin margins” from profits published in 2016 and 2019. The course text presents ratios as a way to compare firms and periods [1]; choosing a valid comparison was the human part. Calculation needed no human; deciding which number to trust did.

The Week 9 capability map tests the same idea against the operating model I designed in Week 4 (Appendix B). That model keeps final order approval with Magnum’s category manager, has staff and AI interpret promotions together, and gives AI the drafting of forecasts and order quantities under human review. Drafting is the kind of task international evidence finds most exposed: clerical work has the highest exposure to generative AI, although the ILO expects transformation rather than replacement [40]. What remains is approval, interpretation and review, which draw on business and meta-capabilities: margin literacy, knowing when a model is wrong, and accountability for a commitment. Seven in ten employers already treat analytical thinking as essential [41]. In Kazakhstan, basic AI skill is becoming common rather than scarce: about 650,000 students completed AI-Sana’s introductory course in its first stage [42]. A graduate’s advantage at Magnum is therefore not using AI but checking it against Magnum’s suppliers, promotions and budgets, the knowledge-worker role the course text describes [1]. Magnum’s entry route fits this: it says it trains new staff itself and runs Magnum Start for students and graduates [36], so it hires people to develop rather than finished specialists.

Carrefour shows what AI at scale does to roles. It deployed Gemini to 250,000 employees in 2025 and uses AI agents in central functions such as sales forecasting and contract management [38]. Its stated aim with Vusion is to automate low value-added tasks and redeploy teams towards customer service [37]. The pattern is redistribution: routine work leaves, while judgment and service work stay. That logic transfers to Kazakhstan, but the scale does not. Carrefour’s integrated stores employ over 300,000 people [37]; Magnum has 9,599 employees and a real revenue fall to absorb [31], [35]. In a firm that size, the person who checks AI output is often the one who must defend it to a manager, and since November 2025 Kazakhstan has an AI Law regulating how such systems are used [27].

The strongest case against my position is that AI removes the junior tasks through which graduates are hired and trained. Payroll data for millions of US workers show employment of 22–25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, mainly through reduced hiring, while experienced workers show no comparable gap [39]. Magnum seems to fit: Forbes’s profile lists headcount falling from 13,509 to 9,599 between the 2023 and 2025 rankings while revenue held [33]. If AI drafts forecasts in my own operating model, the junior analyst who drafted them is no longer needed, and the value goes to experienced managers.

Part of this stands. Yet the same study finds the decline concentrated where AI automates work rather than complements it [39], and my map places graduate value in complementary tasks. Magnum’s headcount fall cannot be attributed to AI: the 13,509 figure could not be checked against a methodology, the 2023 count is rounded, and Kaspi bought control of Magnum’s e-commerce business in 2023 [31]. What survives is narrower: AI may raise the value of each graduate while reducing the number of graduate jobs.

AI will make business graduates more valuable to Magnum on one condition: that they bring the verification and judgment that AI output lacks. Week 8 showed AI right on arithmetic and wrong on meaning; Week 9 showed that Magnum’s operating model keeps exactly those judgments with people. I would change my mind if Magnum’s own figures showed AI-assisted reporting needing no human correction over several reporting periods, or if graduate employment in Kazakhstan’s business occupations began to fall as young workers’ employment has in AI-exposed US occupations. Either would mean the judgment layer is shrinking too.

capreport.title: Executive Summary Report: How Magnum Cash&Carry Should Operate and Compete with AI
capreport.byline: Kniazev Daniil · Group AIB-2602 · 25 October 2026 · Company A: Carrefour · Company B: Magnum Cash&Carry
exec: Magnum Cash&Carry should use AI as a supervised drafting and forecasting layer, not as a decision-maker: pilot demand forecasting and AI-drafted Пайда messages behind named human sign-off, adopt Carrefour-style data controls first, and scale only where measured shelf availability, forecast error and price accuracy beat today’s process. Personalisation from purchase histories is delayed and autonomous order approval is rejected.

Three findings from ten weeks of evidence carry the recommendation. First, Magnum’s 2024 revenue fell to 453.13 billion tenge, 5.6% lower in nominal terms and about 13% lower in real terms [31], [35], so every expansion must be paid for by measured results. Second, each AI test in this portfolio was right on calculation or drafting and wrong on judgment: the Week 6 message offered a delivery channel whose prices were unconfirmed, and the Week 8 interpretation read a rounded headcount as rising productivity. Human review is therefore part of the design, not a temporary safeguard. Third, Carrefour shows the direction, with Gemini deployed to 250,000 employees and AI agents in central functions [38], and also the cost of weak data governance: a €2.25 million CNIL fine [26]. Magnum should take the logic, not the scale.

The 12-month programme costs about 14.9 million tenge ($32,948), 0.003% of 2024 revenue, mostly staff time (Table 3). Year 1 is net negative by design, about 11.5 million tenge, because the pilots buy evidence. Recovered gross margin covers running costs once about 16 branch-categories meet the 98% availability target; one category across all 230 branches would recover about 210 million tenge a year. The weakest assumption is the baseline out-of-stock rate, which Magnum does not publish and the pilot must measure.

Months 0–3 set controls, reconcile stock records and run a four-week message pilot; months 4–8 run the forecasting pilot and extend messaging and finance reporting; months 9–12 scale forecasting to ten branches, test catalogue search and review personalisation readiness. Every initiative has an owner, KPI, cost basis and stop rule (Appendix A). The recommendation changes if stock records cannot be reconciled, which moves forecasting to DELAY, or if Magnum’s measured out-of-stock rate is below about 3%, which narrows the programme to messaging and finance.
blocks: Magnum is a Kazakhstan grocery retailer serving households and business buyers through retail and wholesale [14], with more than 200 stores [3] and, by its careers site, more than 230 branches in 14 cities [36]. Week 1 framed the opportunity around affordability, with annual inflation at 9.8% [4] and e-commerce at 14.3% of retail trade [8]. Four things are now known that Week 1 did not know. Magnum’s 2024 revenue was 453.13 billion tenge with 9,599 employees, down 5.6% on 2023 in nominal terms and 13.1% in real terms [31], [32], [35]. It publishes no financial statements, so profitability, liquidity and debt cannot be assessed from outside (Week 8), and any business case must be validated on internal data. Its footprint has narrowed: the Uzbekistan stores that Week 2 treated as regional experience are being wound down [34], and Kaspi has controlled Magnum’s e-commerce business since 2023 [31]. Finally, the weakest customer touchpoint is the step from promotion to purchase, not the depth of discounts (Week 6). The question is therefore less which AI to buy than which tests Magnum can afford to run, and stop.

Week 2 ranked customers, regulators and employees first; each obligation now maps to a design decision in §4 and §6. Customers need accurate prices and available products, so every AI-drafted message passes an automatic price check and a named sign-off, and search will only show items with checked availability. Regulators set the data boundary: Law 94-V requires consent, storage of personal data in Kazakhstan and conditions for cross-border transfer [7], and the AI Law of November 2025 regulates AI systems and how users are informed [27]. Only public promotion lists and aggregate sales therefore enter AI tools, and personalisation is delayed. Employees must catch errors without pressure to approve them, so they receive training, a recorded right to override a forecast and a quarterly fallback drill. Suppliers need accurate product facts and fair treatment, so Carrefour’s supplier-charter principle is applied through Magnum’s existing corporate rules [21], [22]. Owners need spending that stops when evidence fails, which the stage gates in §8 provide, and communities bear food waste, which becomes a pilot KPI linked to SDG target 12.3 [17]. Two external pressures frame all of this: falling real revenue [31], [35] and a labour market in which routine clerical work is the most exposed to generative AI [40].

Magnum creates value through availability and affordability, and captures it through the margin left after wages, premises and logistics (Weeks 1 and 3). As an LLP its participants’ general meeting is the highest body [18], so a stage-gated programme fits its governance: each expansion is a separate, recorded decision. The proposed operating model does not change how Magnum creates or captures value. It adds no new revenue stream and no paid AI service; it works on the existing model in three places. Fewer empty shelves recover sales that are lost today, clearer promotions convert more of the discount value Magnum already pays for, and checked data reduce waste and correction time. This resolves the potential conflict with §7: the business case counts only recovered gross margin from availability, not revenue from personalisation, which stays delayed, nor unmeasured message effects. The Week 4 matrix allocated one process. Table 2 extends the same four categories across the functions the proposal touches. The rule is the same everywhere: AI may produce a draft, a forecast or a flag, but a named role commits money, sends a message or signs a figure. Fixed rules, not AI, validate inputs and keep logs; staff and AI interpret together where local knowledge matters, such as promotions and supplier constraints. Each function has a review point, an escalation path and a manual fallback, so a failure stops one AI output rather than the business process. Approval authority never moves to software, which is the boundary that makes autonomous ordering a REJECT rather than a later phase.

This allocation constrains the rest of the proposal. Because a named person approves every order and message, the review layer is where the workforce investment goes (§5c): retraining planners, copywriters and analysts rather than hiring AI specialists. Because review takes time, review hours are a cost line in §7 and grow with each scaled branch, which is why break-even depends on reaching about 16 branch-categories. And because each function needs a working fallback before it starts, every roadmap gate in §8 includes a passed fallback drill. Removing human approval would cut cost but would also remove the only control that caught the errors found in Weeks 6 and 8.

In the current state, which still has to be confirmed with staff, the category manager reconciles stock and promotion records by hand before setting quantities; this is the bottleneck, and during promotions recorded stock can differ from shelf stock (Weeks 3 and 5). In the future state fixed rules validate inputs, AI drafts forecasts and quantities, planners and store staff adjust for promotions and delivery days, and the category manager approves every order. The KPI chain runs from here to §7 and §8: shelf availability of at least 98%, a 10% relative reduction in forecast error (WAPE), and 10% less waste value and staff cost per order. Availability drives the §7 benefit, and its baseline is measured in months 0–3 because Magnum does not publish one; the 8.3% world-average out-of-stock rate [43] is only a placeholder. If recorded and shelf stock still differ after reconciliation, forecasting moves to DELAY, as the Week 3 stress test set out. Carrefour tested its SAS forecasting for 18 months before deployment [20], which supports a pilot, not a roll-out.

Magnum’s customers are budget-conscious households, for whom saving is the core value at 9.8% inflation [4]; Magnum Club claims more than two million members [24]. Week 6 found the weak point between consideration and purchase: the Пайда page promised “up to 60%” when the maximum was 53% and offered no next step [23]. The AI-supported draft met all four quality criteria against one for the published text, but checking caught an unconfirmed Magnum Go offer and a non-food deal. Under the proposal customers receive more specific, accurate weekly messages with a clear store or delivery option, written from the public promotion list only. Three controls govern the change: an automatic price check and named sign-off before any send, at least one food staple in every message, and native review of the Kazakh text. The AI-use notice follows legal’s decision under the AI Law [27]. Personalisation stays delayed: Carrefour’s fine for keeping the loyalty data of 28 million inactive customers [26] shows the cost of moving faster than the controls. Message KPIs are tracked but not monetised in §7.

The operating model changes what people do more than how many are needed. It demands three capabilities in the review layer: reading forecast error and margin, applying the four data checks from Week 8 (period, rounding, inflation and scope), and explaining an override to a manager (Week 9). Retrain: in months 0–3 fifteen pilot staff, from the category manager and planner to the copywriters, Kazakh reviewer and CRM and brand managers, receive 16 hours of training and a fallback drill; finance analysts follow in months 4–8 and planners in each scaled branch in months 9–12. Hire or redeploy: one data steward, half-time from month 0 and full-time from month 9, preferably redeployed from IT, owns data reconciliation; no AI specialists are hired in year 1. Redeploy: time saved on manual reconciliation and drafting moves to shelf checks and customer service, the logic Carrefour states for its smart-store programme [37]. Entry routes such as Magnum Start [36] should feed planner and analyst roles in the review layer, because drafting is the most exposed entry task [40] while seven in ten employers treat analytical thinking as essential [41]. No roles are cut in year 1.

The Week 7 register covered one workflow; Appendix C extends it to the whole model. The consolidated position rests on five controls applied in every function. Data boundary: personal data never enter external AI tools, segments are built inside the CRM, and the person responsible for personal data audits prompt logs monthly [7]. Named sign-off: every order, message and reported figure has a recorded approver, in line with NIST’s emphasis on defined roles and responsibilities [16]. Pre-release checks: fixed rules block stale inputs, price mismatches and unflagged discrepancies. Bias rules: a food staple in every message, results compared by language, and forecast error reviewed by branch so that smaller branches are not systematically under-served. Fallback: each function has a manual route, from physical-count orders to message templates and manual reports, practised quarterly. Escalation is uniform: the reviewer stops the output, the function owner decides, IT handles technical faults, the person responsible for personal data handles data issues and legal decides labelling questions. Security rests on ten licensed seats and keeping customer data out of scope. Residual risks are human error under time pressure and the unresolved labelling question under the AI Law [27]; both are tracked rather than assumed away.

Verification follows the standard used throughout the portfolio: isolate one number, find an independent source, compare period, units and entity, and record the outcome even when it disagrees. Applied to AI output, this produced the four checks of Week 8. They found that the arithmetic of an AI-supported interpretation was right while its reading of ranking years, a rounded headcount and old margins was wrong, which is the pattern the assurance design expects in production.

The programme costs about 14.9 million tenge over 12 months (Table 3), 0.003% of 2024 revenue [31]. Most of the cost is people, valued at the Bureau of National Statistics’ wages for Q2 2026: 851,076 tenge a month in ICT and 451,524 tenge in trade [44]; licences are ten standard seats at $20 a month [45] converted at 452.59 tenge per dollar [46]. The return is recovered gross margin from fewer stockouts. With 230 branches [36], an average branch sells about 1.97 billion tenge a year, and a pilot category with an assumed 8% share about 158 million. Industry evidence puts the average out-of-stock rate at 8.3% and the resulting sales loss at 4% [43]; cutting out-of-stocks to 2% recovers about 4.8 million tenge of sales, or 0.91 million tenge of gross margin at 19.1%, Carrefour’s latest margin used as a proxy [2]. If every gate is passed, year 1 returns about 3.4 million tenge, so it is net negative by about 11.5 million. Running costs of 14.0 million tenge a year at ten-branch scale are covered from about 16 branch-categories, so year 2 needs a second category in the ten branches; one category in all 230 branches would return about 210 million tenge a year against 86 million of running cost. The case is most sensitive to Magnum’s actual out-of-stock rate: at 4%, break-even rises to about 48 branch-categories. Nine initiatives sit in three horizons; Appendix A gives all seven required elements for each. Months 0–3 use existing capability and budget: set the governance controls and data boundary; reconcile stock records, measure baselines and train the pilot team; and pilot AI-drafted Пайда messages for four weeks. Months 4–8 depend on that work: the forecasting pilot starts only if records reconcile and the fallback drill is passed, weekly messaging extends only after a 100% price-check pass rate, and AI-assisted finance reporting starts once the data steward controls ledger extracts. Months 9–12 need conditions that do not yet exist: scaling forecasting to ten branches needs 98% availability and a 10% WAPE reduction in the pilot, catalogue search needs reliable availability data, and personalisation is only a readiness review because retention limits, consent and the labelling decision must come first. Every initiative traces to a record: forecasting to Weeks 3–5, messaging to Weeks 6–7, finance reporting to Week 8 and training to Week 9. The first action is the data boundary and stock reconciliation, because every later gate depends on them.

The recommendation rests on robust and contingent assumptions. Robust: named sign-off, the data boundary and the manual fallbacks hold under every published shock category, because they are designed for failure. Contingent: Magnum’s baseline out-of-stock rate must be high enough for forecasting to pay back; below about 3% scaling stops and the programme narrows to messaging and finance. Stock records must reconcile; if not, forecasting moves to DELAY. One AI tool must stay available at about $20 a seat; a cost shock or vendor loss raises break-even but leaves governance unchanged, and templates keep campaigns running. Appendix D sets out, for each shock category, what holds, what changes, what I would abandon and what I would need to know first. My position has narrowed across the term, from “pilot forecasting” in A2 to a portfolio of gated tests whose scale depends on measured availability.

A rehearsed example shows the method. Suppose the AI drafts a Пайда message with a wrong price and it reaches customers. The data boundary and the forecasting pilot still hold, because neither depends on messaging. What changes is that AI messaging pauses, the template fallback takes over and the price check is tested for how the error passed. I would abandon weekly AI messaging until the root cause is fixed, and before restarting I would need to know whether the check failed or was bypassed, because the first is a tool problem and the second a governance one.
